source.title: Bilinear autoencoders find interpretable manifolds
source.authors: Thomas Dooms; Ward Gauderis; Geraint A. Wiggins; José Oramas

record.tranche_reason: The study reports model-activation geometries with multiple dimensions and finds that learned individual latents vary across autoencoder priors, refining the claims about one-dimensional features and canonical dictionary units. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition experiment.
record.gate_note: The empirical geometry and stability analyses in Sections 4.2–4.3 bear on the claim. The paper's theoretical definitions, cited results, and qualitative examples are not treated as independent quantitative findings here. The reconstruction comparison in Section 4.1 is included as an explicit result about how the tested geometric priors capture model activations; figures in Appendix G compare reconstruction across other models but do not directly measure feature geometry. The study does not test toy-model superposition, feature interference, or ordinary SAE feature recovery.
record.test_reason: On Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base activations, the study measures how many dimensions learned dictionary latents need (V6) and whether individual latents agree across sparsity settings and priors (V5). The authors argue both results qualify the one-direction, canonical-unit view. It does not test toy models, neuron polysemanticity, or standard-SAE feature recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that multidimensional geometry is prevalent in LM activations, challenging the linear representation hypothesis. They also say dominant concepts are often approximately linear, with nonlinear surrounding structure. Composite latents recover low-dimensional manifolds with lower reconstruction error. The recovered input subspace is stable across priors and sparsity while individual dictionary entries disagree.
record.recipe_differences: Uses bilinear autoencoders and quadratic/product-space latents rather than the toy-network setup and measurements of Toy Models of Superposition; it does not test superposition or feature interference.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured geometry depends on the structural prior and sparsity: composite latents are mostly low-rank with a higher-dimensional tail, while quadratic latents are consistently high-rank. Similarity also differs between global subspace and per-latent comparisons, and across autoencoder kinds.

fits_no_version.finding: Global subspace spanned by bilinear dictionaries is similar across density settings (79–89% mean off-diagonal; above 90% for similar sparsity) and across prior kinds (79%), even though individual latents differ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different dictionaries recover a stable activation subspace through different, non-canonical decompositions.

record.problems: The main geometry results are for Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base at layer 18; the paper gives qualitative rank summaries rather than numeric prevalence estimates. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these results. The paper notes that its viewer labels were unevaluated and hand-picked geometry examples are qualitative. The latent comparisons do not establish completeness or canonical status for model features.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Appendix G reconstruction plots for Gemma-3-1B and Llama-3.2-1B are not included because they report reconstruction performance rather than directly measuring the claimed feature geometry or feature stability.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-competition test.
No test of other causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of feature spread across neurons and no standard linear SAE recovery test. Reconstruction against a TopK baseline is method performance only.
Completeness and canonicality relative to the model itself are not tested; only cross-run agreement of bilinear dictionaries is measured.
No causal test of whether multidimensional latents are used by the model; no standard SAE comparison of dimensionality.

missing.what: Numeric captured-variance fractions at r=1, 3, 5 and median curves per prior; the text gives only a qualitative summary.
Random-sample viewer examples: many latents primarily linear, others cluster-based; about 10% of latents are dense (qualitative).
Random-initialisation baseline entry for the Hungarian and Frobenius similarity matrices, needed to judge absence against baseline.

record.verdict_notes: V4 links and labels were removed: the rank spectra and reconstruction rows do not measure neuron spread or SAE recovery. R2's full rank is an artifact of the unconstrained quadratic prior. All results come from bilinear, not standard, autoencoders on a single 0.8B model with no uncertainty estimates; Appendix G replicates reconstruction only.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, overcomplete sparse-feature regime, overlapping directions, interference, or sparsity-dependent transition are tested.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or sharing by less important features.
No test of polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.

The study measures bilinear-autoencoder latents on language-model activations, not feature spread across neurons or recovery by a standard linear SAE; it does not assess how comprehensively the latents cover model features.

The study compares learned latent decompositions and subspaces across priors and hyperparameters, but does not establish whether any dictionary is complete or whether its latents are canonical units of the model.
The study measures multidimensional geometry in language-model activations but does not test one-dimensional superposition or compare causal effects of one-dimensional and multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Measured the spectral rank structure of learned composite latents.
rows.measure: Captured variance across top dimensions / latent rank distribution
rows.value: Most composite latents are well-captured by 5 dimensions; with sparsity, most latents are very low rank, with a tail of higher-dimensional structure.
rows.note: The paper reports a low-rank majority but also a tail of higher-dimensional structure; it does not give a numeric fraction in the text.
rows.check: Should not link to V4: a rank spectrum of bilinear latents is not evidence of neuron spread or SAE recovery. For V6, most sparse composite latents are very low rank, but a tail is higher-dimensional, so 1-D holds only partly. The low rank is partly set by the top-K 0.1% constraint on C.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Measured the spectral rank structure of learned quadratic latents.
rows.measure: Captured variance across top dimensions / latent rank distribution
rows.value: Quadratic latents are consistently high-rank; without sparsity, the majority of latents are full-rank.
rows.note: The paper gives this qualitative summary without a numeric proportion.
rows.check: Should not link to V4. Quadratic latents have no constraint on C, so their full rank reflects the unconstrained prior, not the model's features. The authors say this structure 'does not emerge unless explicitly required'. It cannot show multidimensional features, so the record's 'supports' label should be dropped.

rows.check: This compares variants of the study's own method by reconstruction NMSE. Lower error for more expressive priors is confounded by extra capacity, so it cannot isolate multidimensional features. Should not link to V4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The learned dictionaries expose low- and high-dimensional activation geometry in a language model (R1–R3); this is evidence from bilinear dictionaries, not a direct test of standard SAEs.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Compared autoencoder density settings and kinds on Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base
reader_labels.reason: Per-latent similarity is substantially lower than global subspace similarity, including 7% for the cross-kind comparison, which argues against stable canonical individual latents in these settings (R8–R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Global subspace comparisons across density settings and autoencoder kinds
reader_labels.reason: Global similarity is higher than per-latent similarity but varies across comparisons (79%–89% mean off-diagonal in Figure 6); the text also says it is above 90% for similar sparsity levels (R4–R7).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports consistently high-rank quadratic latents and a majority of full-rank latents without sparsity (R2).

reader_labels.label: supports
